text: Heads, I riffle shuffle a sorted deck four times. Tails, a computer shuffles it perfectly. From the deck alone, how often could you tell which? Pick 50, 75, or 100%. Monte Carlo samplers move by random steps, like these riffles. Stop too early, they still remember where they started. The obvious check is the top card. Here's how often each card lands there after four riffles. Only the old top card stands out, one time in 15. Judge by it and you're right, 52% of the time. Four riffles look like plenty. The model cuts near the middle, then drops cards from each half in proportion to its size. Each half stays in order, so one riffle leaves two rising sequences, runs of consecutive cards. Give each sequence its own level. The cut crosses each level once, so a riffle can at most split each level in two. Three riffles. Eight. Four riffles. At most 16, this deck has 14. A perfect shuffle gives 16 or fewer once in 2 million decks. Call 16 or fewer riffled, and you'd be wrong once in 4 million games. The top card can't see this. It lives in the order between cards. Bayer and Diaconis proved that in this model, decks with the same count are equally likely. So pile decks onto their counts. Then every possible deck, weighted by its chance. The red area purple above blue is the distance from random How many more riffles until it below a half A fifth riffle A sixth A seventh Guess riffled where purple is higher. You catch 65% of riffled decks. You also flag 32% of perfect ones. Accuracy is a half plus half the difference, and the difference is the red area. Each riffle roughly halves the gap. Blue's spread, its standard deviation, stays about 2. While the gap spans several spreads, the distance stays near 1. Within one spread, it halves every riffle, that's the cliff. Multiply each gap by 2 to the K, and it settles near 230. Set the gap equal to one spread, and k is just under 7. For n cards, 230 grows like n squared, but the spread like root n, so the cliff sits near 3 halves log base 2 of n. Aldus proved that law. Bayer and Diaconis computed the exact curve. For 52 cards, 7 riffles is the first below a half. Trafethen and Trafethen measured information instead. No cliff. Five or six shuffles do a reasonable job. Many Markov chains share this cliff, and samplers share the trap. One statistic, like the top card, settles long before the whole chain. Back to the coin flip. Three more riffles, and you'd be right only two times out of three. Four riffles fool someone watching the top card, Fooling someone who counts sequences takes 10.
